questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Which condition on a point $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol{x}\in\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$, the finitely generated convex cone of these points?

Let $\boldsymbol{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ have the columns $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Which set equals $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$, the set of all nonnegative linear combinations of these columns?

Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be finitely many points and $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$. Which statement about whether $K$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is correct?
options: $K$ is closed only if $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m$ are linearly independent.
$K$ is closed and also bounded, as it is built from finitely many points.
$K$ is closed only if none of $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m$ is a redundant generator.
$K$ is closed for every choice of the finitely many points $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $m\geq1$. When does the zero vector $\boldsymbol{0}$ belong to $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of these points?
options: Only when some $\boldsymbol{v}_k$ equals $\boldsymbol{0}$, so that $\boldsymbol{0}$ is itself one of the generators.
Always, because the coefficients $\lambda_1=\dots=\lambda_m=0$ are nonnegative and hence allowed.
Only when $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m$ are linearly dependent, so that a nontrivial combination vanishes.
Only when $\boldsymbol{0}\in\operatorname{Conv}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$, so that weights adding up to one give it.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$, let $C=\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be any convex cone that contains all of $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m$. Which relation between $C$ and $K$ always holds?
options: $C\subseteq K$ holds only when $K$ is closed.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(2,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,3)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which point lies in $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of $\boldsymbol{v}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2$?

Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(1,-1)$. Which coefficients $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ write $\boldsymbol{y}=(5,1)$ as $\lambda_1\boldsymbol{v}_1+\lambda_2\boldsymbol{v}_2$, showing that $\boldsymbol{y}\in\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$?

Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,2)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(-1,-2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which set is $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of $\boldsymbol{v}_1$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2$?
Let $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\{(2,1),(0,1)\})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be the set of nonnegative linear combinations of $(2,1)$ and $(0,1)$. Which list of points generates the same cone $K$?

Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,0)$, $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(0,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,-1)=2\boldsymbol{v}_1-\boldsymbol{v}_2$. Where does $\boldsymbol{y}$ lie with respect to the convex hull, the cone and the span of $\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\}$?
options: In $\operatorname{Conv}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$, as its coefficients $2$ and $-1$ add up to $1$
Outside $\operatorname{span}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2\})$, as it has a negative coordinate

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_7\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and let $\boldsymbol{x}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ lie in $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_7\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of these points. Which statement about writing $\boldsymbol{x}$ with fewer generators always holds?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}$ is a nonnegative linear combination of exactly three of the $\boldsymbol{v}_k$, never of fewer.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ is a nonnegative linear combination of at most three linearly independent $\boldsymbol{v}_k$.
At most three $\boldsymbol{v}_k$ suffice only with real coefficients; with nonnegative ones all seven may be needed.
$\boldsymbol{x}$ is a nonnegative linear combination of at most two of the $\boldsymbol{v}_k$.

questions.question: To prove that $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})$ is closed, one writes $K$ as the union of the cones generated by the linearly independent subsets of $\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\}$ and shows that each of these cones is closed. Why is $K$ then closed?
options: There are only finitely many such subsets, and a finite union of closed sets is closed.
Each piece is closed, and a union of closed sets is closed however many sets it has.
The pieces are pairwise disjoint closed sets, and a disjoint union of closed sets is closed.
Each piece is closed and bounded, so the union is compact and therefore closed.

questions.question: Let $K=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1>0,\ x_2>0\}\cup\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, the open positive quadrant together with the origin. Is $K$ a finitely generated convex cone, and why?
options: Yes: $K$ equals $\operatorname{Cone}(\{(1,0),(0,1)\})$, the cone of the two unit vectors.
No: $K$ is not a convex cone, because the origin is cut off from the rest of $K$.
Yes: $K$ is cut out by finitely many linear inequalities, so it is polyhedral and finitely generated.
No: $K$ is not closed, whereas every finitely generated convex cone is closed.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,0)$, $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(0,1)$, $\boldsymbol{v}_3=(1,2)$; then $\boldsymbol{x}=(2,3)=\sum_k\lambda_k\boldsymbol{v}_k$ with $\boldsymbol{\lambda}=(1,1,1)$, and $\sum_k\mu_k\boldsymbol{v}_k=\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{\mu}=(1,2,-1)$. A reduction step sets $\lambda_k'=\lambda_k-t\mu_k$ with $t=\min\{\lambda_k/\mu_k\colon\mu_k>0\}$. What is $\boldsymbol{\lambda}'$?

Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,0,0)$, $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(0,1,0)$, $\boldsymbol{v}_3=(1,1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\boldsymbol{y}=(a,2,1)$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}$. For which values of $a$ does $\boldsymbol{y}$ lie in $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of the three points?
Let $K=\operatorname{Cone}(\{(1,2),(2,1)\})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be the set of nonnegative linear combinations of $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$. Which description of $K$ by linear inequalities is correct?

In the closedness proof for $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, the coefficients of $\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}$ are $\boldsymbol{u}=(\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$, where the columns of $\boldsymbol{B}$ are generators. Why does this fail if $m>n$ and all generators are columns?
options: The product $\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B}$ is not a square matrix when $m>n$, so it cannot be inverted.
A cone generated by more than $n$ points need not be closed, so the formula cannot prove it.
The formula would still give the unique coefficients of $\boldsymbol{y}$, but some might be negative.
More than $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are linearly dependent, so $\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B}$ is singular.

questions.question: For points $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\geq1$, how is the condition $m\geq n+1$ related to $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_m\})=\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, to the nonnegative linear combinations of the points filling the whole space?
options: $m\geq n+1$ is both necessary and sufficient for the cone to be all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$m\geq n+1$ is not necessary: $n$ generators spanning $\mathbb{R}^n$ already fill $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$m\geq n+1$ is necessary for the cone to be all of $\mathbb{R}^n$, but not sufficient.
$m\geq n+1$ is too weak: filling $\mathbb{R}^n$ requires $m\geq2n$, one generator per $\pm\boldsymbol{e}_i$.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1=(1,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{v}_2=(-1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which third point $\boldsymbol{v}_3$ makes $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3\})$, the set of nonnegative linear combinations of the three points, equal to all of $\mathbb{R}^2$?

Let $\boldsymbol{B}$ have the columns $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$, and let $\boldsymbol{y}=(1,1,0)$. A student finds $\boldsymbol{u}=(\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}=(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3})\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Is $\boldsymbol{y}$ in the cone $\{\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}\colon\boldsymbol{u}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, and why?
options: Not in the cone: $\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{y}$ forces $u_1=u_2=1$ from rows one and two, but then row three gives $2\neq0$.
In the cone: with independent columns the formula returns the $\boldsymbol{u}$ with $\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{y}$, and $\boldsymbol{u}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$.
Not in the cone: the formula requires a square $\boldsymbol{B}$, and this $\boldsymbol{B}$ is $3\times2$, so it cannot be used.
In the cone: $\boldsymbol{y}$ and both columns have nonnegative coordinates, so nonnegative weights reach $\boldsymbol{y}$.
